questions.text: An architect proposes using a Doric colonnade on a new shopping center but claims it is 'contextual Post-Modernism.' A critic argues it may actually be Neo-Classicism. Which evaluation framework resolves this dispute?

options.text: Check if the columns are load-bearing — Post-Modern columns are always non-structural applied ornament, which is a key distinction
Check the date of construction — all work after 1972 using Classical elements is automatically Post-Modern, according to some theorists
Determine whether the colonnade is used ironically, out of scale, or in jarring combinations versus sincerely and proportionally
Identify whether the architect is in Jencks's canon — only work by listed architects qualifies as Post-Modern, according to his criteria

rationale.summary: The resolution is whether Classical elements are used ironically and out of proportion (Post-Modern) vs. sincerely and proportionally (Neo-Classical).
rationale.explanation: The article's Trap 1 provides the evaluative framework: Post-Modernism uses Classical elements 'ironically, out of scale, in unexpected colors, or in jarring combinations.' Neo-Classicism uses them 'sincerely and proportionally.' The intent and execution — not the date or structural role — determine classification.
common_misconceptions: Date of construction is not the classifier — sincerity vs. irony in the use of historical elements is
Many Post-Modern columns are structurally irrelevant, but so are many Neo-Classical columns — this is not diagnostic

questions.explanation: Tests application of the Post-Modern vs. Neo-Classical evaluative framework to a realistic design scenario.

questions.text: Robert Venturi's phrase 'Less is a bore' was a direct response to which architect's philosophy, and where did it first appear?

Frank Lloyd Wright's 'organic architecture'; it appeared in Venturi's Complexity and Contradiction (1966)
Mies van der Rohe's 'Less is More'; it appeared in Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966)
Louis Sullivan's 'Form follows function'; it appeared in The Language of Post-Modern Architecture (1977)

rationale.summary: Venturi's 'Less is a bore' directly countered Mies's 'Less is More' in Complexity and Contradiction (1966).
rationale.explanation: The article states: 'Where Mies said Less is More, Robert Venturi countered: Less is a bore.' The table confirms the book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) is 'the theoretical manifesto of Post-Modernism; challenged Mies's Less is More with Less is a bore.'
common_misconceptions: Learning from Las Vegas (1972) is Venturi and Scott Brown's second major book — the phrase is from Complexity and Contradiction (1966)
Sullivan's phrase is about function determining form — unrelated to Venturi's argument against Miesian minimalism

questions.explanation: Tests recall of the Venturi-Mies intellectual confrontation and its publication source.

rationale.summary: The Vanna Venturi House has a split gable, oversized chimney, and distorted Classical references.
rationale.explanation: The article's table describes the Vanna Venturi House as 'a deliberately contradictory house with a split gable, oversized chimney, and distorted Classical references.' questions.text: In Learning from Las Vegas (1972), Venturi and Scott Brown propose two building types. Which statement correctly defines the 'Duck'?

options.text: A conventional structural box with signs, ornament, and symbolic decoration applied to its exterior surfaces
A building that uses double coding to appeal simultaneously to popular taste and elite architectural audiences
A building whose overall three-dimensional form itself acts as the primary symbol of its function or identity
A high-tech building that exposes its mechanical systems as decorative ornament on the exterior facade

rationale.summary: The Duck is a building whose entire form is itself the symbol.
rationale.explanation: The article states: 'the Duck (where the building's form itself is the symbol — e.g., a building shaped like a duck).' Venturi and Scott Brown's mnemonic in the article: 'DUCK = form IS symbol; SHED = form HAS symbol.' The Decorated Shed (Option A) is the box with applied ornament.
common_misconceptions: LEA Trap 3: The Duck is the form-as-symbol; the Decorated Shed is the box with applied ornament — these are frequently swapped
Double Coding (Option C) is Charles Jencks's concept, not the definition of the Duck

questions.explanation: Tests the Duck vs. Decorated Shed distinction — the documented LEA Trap 3 in the article.

questions.text: Charles Jencks declared the symbolic death of Modern Architecture occurred on July 15, 1972. What event did he associate with this date?

options.text: The demolition of Pruitt-Igoe public housing in St. Louis — a failed Modernist social housing megaproject
The completion of the Centre Pompidou in Paris, which Jencks said marked the end of Modernist restraint
The publication of Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture, ending Modernism's intellectual dominance
The opening of Philip Johnson's AT&T Building in New York, which shocked the Modernist architectural establishment

rationale.summary: Jencks associated July 15, 1972 with the demolition of the Pruitt-Igoe housing complex in St. Louis.
rationale.explanation: The article states Jencks 'declared the death of Modern Architecture on July 15, 1972 (the demolition of Pruitt-Igoe).' He published this claim in The Language of Post-Modern Architecture (1977). Pruitt-Igoe was designed by Minoru Yamasaki, completed 1956, demolished 1972 — a failed Modernist social housing project.
common_misconceptions: The AT&T Building (Option D) was completed in 1984 — twelve years after the declared death of Modernism
Complexity and Contradiction (1966) predates the 1972 date by six years

questions.explanation: Tests recall of Jencks's symbolic date and event for the death of Modern Architecture.
